intro: Many people first meet martial arts on a screen. A 1943 Japanese film retold judo's early rivals, a 1984 American film sent children to karate schools, and Thai and Indonesian films carried muay boran and pencak silat around the world. Films invent schools, names and costumes. Real schools then have to answer students who arrive asking for them.

In the same decades, a new institution grew up: mixed martial arts. It drew on older mixed contests in Greece, Brazil and Japan. In the United States it began in 1993 as a pay-per-view show with few rules. State athletic commissions, first built to license boxing, later wrote its rule book and licensed its fighters.

In this unit you will separate film names from school names and trace a league from its first event to its fifty-state approval. By the end, you can name the films, companies, laws and commissions involved. You can also explain the difference between an invented name, a documented new style and a regulated league.
bigQuestion: When films and promoters create new names for fighting arts, what records show who really built a style or a league?

write.prompt: Is mixed martial arts better described as an old art or a modern league? Argue from at least three records in this unit: for example, Philostratus on pankration, the 1993 UFC 1 event, the 2001 Unified Rules or New York's 2016 law. Then compare one film-made name, such as Cobra Kai, with one documented style, such as Kajukenbo.
tips: Name each record with its date, place or body.
Keep film stories and school records in separate sentences.
Attribute claims to the promoter, studio or historian who made them.
Use unit terms such as lineage, sanctioned and athletic commission.
